English_Gloss: Matrilineal clan / Extended family / Kinship unit
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The corporate matrilineal kin group; the fundamental ontological unit of identity, mutual insurance, and moral accountability in Akan society.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Invoked to resolve internal disputes, demand mutual loyalty, and mandate funerary/crisis participation.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Abusua te sɛ kwaeɛ, wowɔ akyire a ɛyɛ kusuu, wokɔ mu a na wohunu sɛ dua biara si ne siberɛ.
Proverb_Translation: The family is like a forest: from afar it looks dense and indivisible, but inside every tree stands in its own place.

English_Gloss: Mutual cooperative labor / Reciprocal farm assistance
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Traditional rotating communal labor system where community members cultivate each other's farms without wages, embodying relational mutualism.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Used to mobilize community members for communal projects, civic duties, or mutual aid.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Nsa baako nkura adesoa.
Proverb_Translation: One hand alone cannot carry a heavy load.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The harmonious integration of disparate community members into an undivided collective whole; foundational to consensus democracy.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Core rhetorical trope in chieftaincy arbitration, national solidarity appeals, and town councils.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Nkabom mu na ahoɔden wɔ.
Proverb_Translation: In unity lies indestructible collective strength.

English_Gloss: Oneness / Collective solidarity / Acting in unison
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Unified collective agency prioritizing community well-being over sectional or egoistic interests.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Applied to encourage teamwork and eliminate interpersonal factionalism.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Baanu so a, emmia.
Proverb_Translation: When two people carry a heavy load together, it does not pinch or crush them.

English_Gloss: Every human is the sibling of human / Universal humanism
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The moral apex of Akan philosophy (Gyekye/Wiredu): every human possesses divine dignity (Okra) and is entitled to kinship obligations.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Invoked as the highest moral argument for hospitality, stranger protection, and humanitarian assistance.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Onipa nua ne nipa; obi nnyaa ne yɔnko wɔ amanehunu mu.
Proverb_Translation: A fellow human is one's sibling; no one should abandon their fellow traveler in distress.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Spontaneous benevolence and deep visceral empathy toward community members in hardship.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Pinnacle virtue expected of chiefs, wealthy benefactors, and community elders.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ayamye nti na aboa adanko kɔe kɔtoo n'asaso mu.
Proverb_Translation: It is out of pure benevolence that the hare gave up its shelter.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Active relational maintenance that weaves non-kin individuals into dependable social networks.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Refers to steadfast, multi-generational familial and peer alliances.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ayɔnkofa pa na ɛma abusua tim.
Proverb_Translation: Enduring fellowship is what stabilizes the extended community.

English_Gloss: Civic warrior group / Communal youth association
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Traditional civic and military organizations responsible for community defense, disaster management, and public works.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Invoked during communal labor, civic emergencies, and traditional festivals.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Asafo kɔ a, wɔkɔ biako.
Proverb_Translation: When the communal company marches, it moves as a unified body.

English_Gloss: The public / Humanity / The entire commonwealth
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The collective body of humanity or the nation, whose welfare supersedes any private ambition.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Used in civic debates, royal declarations, and public service ethics.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Amansan nyinaa yɛ Onyame mma.
Proverb_Translation: All citizens of the commonwealth are the children of God.

English_Gloss: Communal consultation / Deliberative caucus / Consensus council
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The formal caucus in Akan governance where leaders deliberate behind closed doors until unanimous consensus is achieved.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Invoked in family inheritance meetings, court trials, and community arbitrations.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Agyinatuo mu na asɛm gye.
Proverb_Translation: It is in collective deliberative caucus that difficult disputes are resolved.

English_Gloss: Selfishness / Greed / Solitary grasping / Extreme individualism
Morphology_Root: pɛ (want) + sɛ (that) + me (I) + nko (alone) + minya (I get)
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Pathologized individualism where personal accumulation occurs at the expense of communal welfare; viewed as moral decay.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Severe social reproach applied to corrupt leaders, ungenerous kin, or resource hoarders.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Pɛsɛmenkominyafoɔ kɔ akuraa a, ɔno nko na ɔwe akokɔ.
Proverb_Translation: When the selfish man goes to the village, he eats the whole chicken alone in isolation.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Elevating oneself above others in defiance of social hierarchy, humility norms, and collective equality.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Warns individuals against boasting or displaying contempt toward elders or peers.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ahomasoɔ de brɛbrɛ kɔ owuo mu.
Proverb_Translation: Arrogant self-exaltation marches steadily and inevitably toward ruin and death.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Flamboyant display of wealth or achievements that breaches communal egalitarian values and breeds resentment.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Used to counsel against conspicuous consumption and flashy boastfulness.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ahododoɔfoɔ tɔ nsuo mu a, obi nnye no.
Proverb_Translation: When the boastful show-off falls into deep waters, onlookers hesitate to rescue him.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Excessive love and indulgence of one's own physical self and desires to the neglect of communal duties.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Used to caution against frivolous living and self-centered spending.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ahopɛ dodoɔ na ɛde ohia ba.
Proverb_Translation: Excessive self-pampering and pleasure-seeking breeds poverty.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Disregarding collective advice or elder guidance in favor of stubborn self-determination.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Applied to rebellious youth or stubborn adults who refuse familial mediation.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Me ara me pɛ de onipa kɔ asɛm kɛseɛ mu.
Proverb_Translation: Insisting on 'my own will alone' leads a person into catastrophe.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Insatiable lust for the possessions of others, undermining social trust and equity.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Used in dispute resolutions involving theft, boundary disputes, or inheritance.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Anikonkrɔn de abususɛm ba.
Proverb_Translation: Covetous greed breeds devastating internal strife within the clan.

English_Gloss: Jealousy / Malicious envy / Resentment of peer success
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Internal bitterness experienced when another community member prospers; seen as the root of witchcraft and spiritual malice.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Invoked to warn against competing with siblings or neighbors.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ahoɔyaw de owuo ba.
Proverb_Translation: Bitter envy breeds death and destruction.

English_Gloss: Greed for free goods / Gluttony / Parasitic grasping
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Craving to consume benefits of communal labor without contributing reciprocal effort.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Used against opportunists who exploit communal hospitality.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Adifudepɛfoɔ kɔ afahyɛ a, ɔhwere n'animuonyam.
Proverb_Translation: The parasitic glutton attends the festival and loses all his public dignity.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Supreme Akan title of deference, uniting living monarchs, grandparents, and deified ancestors (Nsamanfoɔ) in a continuous cosmological chain.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Mandatory address for chiefs, queenmothers, and biological/classificatory grandparents.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Nana Nyame na ɔwɔ asase ne emu nnoɔma nyinaa.
Proverb_Translation: Sovereign God possesses the earth and everything therein.

English_Gloss: Elder / Moral arbiter / Person of maturity and wisdom
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: A status achieved through chronological maturity, ethical character, wisdom, and recognized arbitral capacity.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Applied to heads of families, village elders, and respected arbiters.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Opanyin nni fie a, mmofra didi abɔntene.
Proverb_Translation: When the elder is absent from the home, children eat disorderly out in the open street.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The moral duty of acknowledging and yielding to age, rank, wisdom, and sacred authority.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Fundamental prerequisite in the moral socialization of Akan children.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Wobu opanyin a, wokora wo ankasa wo daakye so.
Proverb_Translation: When you respect an elder, you safeguard your own future elderhood.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Voluntary restraint of ego to honor elders, superiors, and collective cohesion.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Expected posture when appearing before chiefs, in-laws, or family councils.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ahobraseɛ na ɛde animuonyam ba.
Proverb_Translation: Humility is what ushers in enduring glory and social esteem.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Faithful, humble dedication to chiefs, elders, deities, and community institutions.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Describes royal courtiers, religious acolytes, and apprentices.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Wosom panin a, wonya panin adikan.
Proverb_Translation: If you serve an elder with devotion, you earn the right to lead as an elder in turn.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The diplomatic bridge between ruler and people; filters raw speech into poetic, refined court language.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Direct unmediated address to a king is taboo; all dialogue must pass through the Okyeame.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ɔhene nni aso; ɔkyeame na ɔte asɛm ma no.
Proverb_Translation: The king has no direct public ears; the linguist listens and articulates on his behalf.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The sacred custodian of the ancestral stool, embodying military, judicial, and spiritual leadership.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Addressed with utmost ceremonial deference (*Nana Ohene*).
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ɔhene nya ahotenafoɔ pa a, ne man gye mpuntuo.
Proverb_Translation: When a king is surrounded by wise counselors, his nation flourishes.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The co-ruler and kingmaker who nominates the chief, arbitrates family and women's affairs, and serves as the ultimate moral compass.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Possesses decisive veto power in royal succession disputes.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ɔhemaa na ɔnim obi a ɔfata akonnwa no.
Proverb_Translation: It is the queenmother who knows the legitimate heir worthy of the stool.

English_Gloss: Solemn royal majesty / Grandeur / Court solemnity
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The intimidating grandeur and sacred aura surrounding the palace and the occupant of the Golden Stool.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Describes the atmosphere during royal durbars and State festivals.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ahemfie kuntunkruni ma obubuafoɔ mpo bɔ ne bra bɔkɔɔ.
Proverb_Translation: The solemn grandeur of the royal palace makes even the boastful walk with reverence.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Kneeling before royalty or elders when making petitions, expressing repentance, or swearing allegiance.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Physical greeting etiquette required when approaching high chiefs.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Nkotodwe-gu na ɛtwe abufuo firi ɔpanyin bo.
Proverb_Translation: Humble genuflection removes wrath from the heart of the elder.

Morphology_Root: akyi (back/turn away) + wa + deɛ (thing turned away from)
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Deed abhorred by deities, ancestors, and society; breaching it incurs severe cosmic pollution and social sanction.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Categorizes incest, suicide, insult to monarch, farming on sacred taboo days (e.g. Dabɔne).
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Sɛ wodi akyiwadeɛ a, wobɔ wo nsam gu wo man so.
Proverb_Translation: If you commit a taboo, you pour misfortune over your entire community.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: A violation of cosmic order so severe that it threatens the collective existence unless ritually cleansed.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Applied when crimes require ritual pacification and animal sacrifice (*Asubɔ*).
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ɔbra bɔne de musuo ba fie.
Proverb_Translation: Corrupt moral conduct brings spiritual abomination into the homestead.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The habituated moral nature of a person; the defining metric determining whether one is truly an 'onipa' (moral person).
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Primary consideration in marriage proposals, chieftaincy enstoolment, and hiring.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Suban pa na ɛkyɛn ahoɔfɛ.
Proverb_Translation: Good moral character is far more precious than physical beauty.

English_Gloss: Sacred taboo day / Non-working ritual day
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Specific days in the Akan 42-day calendar (Adae, Fofie, Awukudae) dedicated to ancestral communion where farming or tilling the earth is strictly forbidden.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Breaching Dabɔne farming taboos incurs heavy fines and sacrificial sheep penalties.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Obi nkɔ asase so wɔ Dabɔne.
Proverb_Translation: No one goes to till the sacred soil on a sacred taboo day.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Sacred lustrations performed to cleanse people, royal stools, or land from moral and taboo contamination.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Central rite of the annual Odwira festival and post-taboo rehabilitation.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Asubɔ na ɛhohoro musuo gu.
Proverb_Translation: Ritual purification is what washes away calamity and spiritual stain.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Hard-headed rebellion against elder counsel and established societal norms.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Used in reprimanding deviant youth who disregard customary rules.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ti-ɛdenfoɔ kɔ asuo a, ɔde ahina bɔbo.
Proverb_Translation: The stubborn person goes to the river and returns with a shattered clay pot.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Literal 'hard-earedness'—refusal to listen to admonition, leading to social isolation and downfall.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Standard descriptor for non-conformists and rule-breakers.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Asoɔden de mmɔborɔhunu ba.
Proverb_Translation: Disobedience inevitably yields misery and regret.

Morphology_Root: aso (ear) + twe (pulling / pulling by the ears)
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Formal disciplinary measures imposed by family heads or traditional courts to correct errant members.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Applied to customary fines, banishment, or physical discipline.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Asotwe pa ma ɔba nya suban pa.
Proverb_Translation: Righteous discipline gives a child good character.

English_Gloss: Reverence for God / Moral conscience rooted in Divine awe
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The interiorized moral fear of God's universal justice, serving as an omnipresent internal inhibitor against secret sins.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Considered the ultimate foundation of trustworthy character (*Onipa a ɔwɔ Nyamesuro*).
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Nyamesuro ne nyansa nyinaa mfitiaseɛ.
Proverb_Translation: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of all true wisdom.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Invocation of a tragic historical calamity of a royal lineage; serves as an immediate injunction halting dispute actions until court review.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Customary legal injunction (e.g. *Ntamkɛseɛ* - The Great Oath of Asante).
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Woka ntan a, wodi ho adanseɛ wɔ badwa mu.
Proverb_Translation: When you swear an oath, you must bear testimony and abide by the judgment of the assembly.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Literal 'brightness of the face'; the spiritual and moral charisma radiating from integrity, ancestral favor, and community respect.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Bestowed upon leaders, virtuous citizens, and benefactors.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Dintiti pa kyɛn ahonyadeɛ.
Proverb_Translation: A good, untarnished name is greater than vast material fortunes.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The deep psychological aversion to public disgrace; acts as the internal regulatory conscience preventing unethical behavior.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Communal mechanism for self-policing without external police presence.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Fɛre nni aduro.
Proverb_Translation: There is no medicinal herb that can wipe away the stain of public shame.

English_Gloss: Disgrace / Public humiliation / Contempt / Diminishing face
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Diminishing someone's public dignity through disrespect or exposure of fault.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Used when reprimanding public insults, mocking elders, or slander.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Mma obiara mmɔ wo animtia wɔ bagua mu.
Proverb_Translation: Do not invite public humiliation upon yourself before the gathered council.

English_Gloss: Ignominy / Total social disgrace / Ruin of face
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Total loss of honor and moral standing in the public sphere, bringing shame to the entire clan (*Abusua*).
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Core Akan honor code motto expressing that physical death is superior to dishonor.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Owuo pa sen anim-guaseɛ.
Proverb_Translation: An honorable death is far preferable to living in public disgrace.

English_Gloss: Spotless reputation / Great name / Enduring integrity
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: A sterling moral reputation accumulated over generations that provides social capital and blessing to one's descendants.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Invoked to discourage shady shortcuts to wealth.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Din pa na ɛdi bem wɔ ahemfie.
Proverb_Translation: A good name is acquitted without difficulty in the royal palace.

Morphology_Root: ani (eye/presence) + da-ho (lying in place / remaining steady)
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Maintaining calm, dignified poise in the face of provocation or difficulty without losing self-control.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Expected of judges, spokespersons, and parents.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Anidaho ma onipa kɔ so di panyin.
Proverb_Translation: Dignified self-restraint maintains a person's standing as a mature elder.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Artfully indirect language used to convey hard truths without causing offense or breaching status hierarchy.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Vital in diplomatic missions, marriage negotiations, and royal discourse.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ɔpanyin kasa a, ɔka no kasakoa mu na amaneɛ ansɛe.
Proverb_Translation: When an elder speaks, he uses subtle nuance and circumlocution to preserve harmony.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The condensed distillation of historical and moral wisdom; used as indirect rhetorical tools to persuade, reprimand, and resolve conflicts.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Required element of eloquent Akan public address (*Kasa pa*).
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ɔbadwemma na wɔbɔ no bɛ, na wɔnnkã asɛm mprɔprɔ nnkyerɛ no.
Proverb_Translation: A wise child is addressed in proverbs, not through raw, blunt speech.

English_Gloss: Gentle speech / Soft, tempered speech / Diplomatic tone
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Speech delivered with calmness and tact to pacify anger and prevent rupture in social ties.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Counsel given to disputants during arbitration.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Kasa bɔkɔɔ dwudwo abufuo ano.
Proverb_Translation: Soft and gentle speech cools the fiercest wrath.

English_Gloss: Raw speech / Blunt aggressive speech / Uncouth language
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Speaking bluntly without diplomatic framing or proverbial cushion; considered immature and offensive in Akan oratorical ethics.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Severely reprimanded in courtroom proceedings and marriage mediation.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Kasa-mprɔprɔ de ntɔkwa ba badwa mu.
Proverb_Translation: Blunt, unfiltered speech causes brawls in the assembly.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: A carefully weighed, pregnant sentence whose brevity conveys vast contextual weight and authority.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Used when an elder settles a protracted dispute with a concise, decisive verdict.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Ɔpanin kasafua baako pɛ gye ɔman.
Proverb_Translation: A single weighed word from an elder can save an entire nation.

English_Gloss: Consulting an elder / Seeking seasoned counsel
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The mandatory cultural protocol of seeking elder verification before initiating marriage, land purchase, or public statements.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Pre-condition in Akan customary transactional law.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Wobisa panyin a, womfom kwan.
Proverb_Translation: If you inquire of the elder, you never lose your pathway.

English_Gloss: Divine Soul / Inner destiny / Spark of Supreme Being
Morphology_Root: kra (to bid farewell / to receive divine mandate from Nyame)
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The divine essence bestowed directly by Onyame; carries an individual's pre-destined fate (Nkrabea) and intrinsic human dignity.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: The source of unconditional moral worth in Akan humanism.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Obi nkra Nyame na ɔnkyerɛ no.
Proverb_Translation: No one teaches another how to receive destiny from God; every soul is independently accountable to God.

Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The experiential, moral, and dynamic spirit inherited from the father (Ntɔro); determines one's psychological strength and moral character.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Used in evaluating charismatic leadership (*Sunsum kɛseɛ* / *Sunsum duru*).
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Sunsum duru na ɛtumi fa asɛm ho.
Proverb_Translation: A weighty, formidable spirit is what withstands adversity and witchcraft.

English_Gloss: Blood / Maternal biological essence / Clan foundation
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The physical substance transmitted solely by mothers that forms the biological basis of the *Abusua* (clan) and citizenship.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Legal determinant of Akan inheritance and royal stool succession.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Mogya yɛ duru sen nsuo.
Proverb_Translation: Blood is thicker than water.

English_Gloss: Paternal spirit group / Patrilineal moral archetype
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: The spiritual grouping passed from father to child, determining moral temperament, taboo observances (Akyiwadeɛ), and greeting responses (*Yaa Agya*, *Yaa Asɔn*).
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Determines daily conversational greeting etiquette across Akan subgroups.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Agya ntɔro na ɛbɔ ɔba ho ban.
Proverb_Translation: The father's spirit provides spiritual protection for the child.

English_Gloss: Ancestors / The living-dead / Guardians of morality
Cultural_Psychological_Definition: Departed elders who lived virtuous lives, now existing as spiritual intermediaries and enforcers of custom, law, and morality.
Context_Pragmatic_Usage: Libations (*Nsaguo*) are poured to them at every public state or family ceremony.
Sample_Proverb_Expression: Nsamanfoɔ ani da hɔ; wɔhunu adeɛ nyinaa.
Proverb_Translation: The ancestors are ever watchful; they perceive all secret actions.
